english: Know prakṛti (primal matter) and puruṣa, here the jīva (individual self), as both beginningless, and know the vikāra (modifications) and the guṇa (qualities), sattva (clarity) and the rest, as born of prakṛti. Everything other than Īśvara (the Lord), conscious and non-conscious alike, is the kṣetra (field), and it is summed up here because the next topic is the One who impels it, and the impeller cannot be described until what He impels is known. The guṇa are named apart from the vikāra, though they too arise from prakṛti, because they are both effect and not effect, their arising out of dissolution into creation being very slight, as the Mādhucchandasa recension says.
divergence_note: Read with Jayatīrtha's Prameyadīpikā on Madhva's bhāṣya (their 13.20): Madhva frames the verse as preparing for 'from what, what' (13.4), says the guṇa (qualities) are sattva (clarity) and the rest, and explains that the vikāra (modifications) are listed separately because the guṇa differ from them only very slightly in passing from laya (dissolution) to sarga (creation), citing a Mādhucchandasa text that calls the three both effect and not effect. Jayatīrtha adds the doctrinally weighty points. He reads 'from what, what' as the nature of the preraka (impeller), and argues that describing the impeller needs prior knowledge of the prerya (what is impelled), which is the field with its kinds; hence it is summed up here, not earlier, which would have been prolix. He states that everything other than Īśvara (the Lord), conscious and non-conscious, is called kṣetra (field); that prakṛti (primal matter) here means the twenty-four principles listed from the great elements on; that vikāra covers all modifications, the three guṇa included, set apart only by a particular intention; and that puruṣa here means the jīva (individual self). He also says the sum is brief because the theme returns at 13.26, and rejects the reading of guṇa as pleasure, pain and delusion (marked in the edition as Śaṅkara), since those are already among the modifications and listing them again would be improper. Neither commentator glosses anādi (beginningless), which is rendered as the verse says. The others differ sharply: Advaita and Advaita-bhakti read the guṇa as pleasure, pain and delusion, the reading Jayatīrtha rejects; Viśiṣṭādvaita takes the guṇa as the virtues that lead to release; Śuddhādvaita and Bhakti make prakṛti the power and the puruṣa a portion of the Lord. Dvaita places the jīva inside the field and the Lord outside it as its impeller.
everyday_application: Before you work out who is really steering an organization, map everything that is being steered, and put yourself and the other people on that map along with the machinery. A consultant who leaves themselves off the chart will misread who is moving whom, and it also pays to keep near-identical categories apart, such as a company's basic culture and the particular habits it has produced, rather than letting one stand in for the other.
